1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
13	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
14	- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
15	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
16	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
17	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
18	
19	## How to commit
20	
21	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
22	
23	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
24	
25	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
26	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
27	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
28	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
29	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
30	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
31	
32	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
33	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
34	
35	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
36	
37	## Pushing
38	
39	Push after every commit.
40	
41	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
42	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree leaves its branch. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
43	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
44	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
45	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
46	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
47	
48	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
49	
50	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The platform rebuilds a lost container from `blinded-fable`.
51	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
52	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
53

1	# Running tests
2	
3	**track**
4	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.
5	
6	**shard**
7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
8	
9	**code state**
10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.
11	
12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
20	
21	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
22	
23	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
24	
25	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
26	
27	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
28	
29	The two suites work in the same way:
30	
31	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
32	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
33	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
34	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
35	
36	To run a suite:
37	
38	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
39	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
40	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
41	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
42	
43	## The switches that the harness reads
44	
45	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
46	
47	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
48	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
49	- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
50	- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
51	- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
52	- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.
53	
54	## Outside the gate
55	
56	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
57	- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
58	  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
59	  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
60	  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
61	  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
62	  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
63	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).
64	
65	## When to run a whole suite
66	
67	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
68	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
69	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
70	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
71	  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
72	- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
73	- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
74	- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the runtime (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
75	- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.
76	
77	The suites do not check these:
78	
79	- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
80	- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
81	- the linker's aliasing of apis;
82	- `fortress unparse`;
83	- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
84	- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.
85	
86	If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.
87	
88	## One test, or a few
89	
90	Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.
91	
92	### Interpreter tests
93	
94	Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
95	
96	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
97	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
98	
99	- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
100	- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
101	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
102	- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
103	- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
104	- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
105	- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.
106	
107	To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:
108	
109	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss
110	
111	The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").
112	
113	### Compiled tests
114	
115	Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).
116	
117	The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.
118	
119	    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
120	        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1
121	
122	- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
123	- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
124	- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
125	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
126	- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
127	- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.
128	
129	To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:
130	
131	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test
132	
133	Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.
134	
135	## One unit-test class, or one track
136	
137	To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.
138	
139	To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:
140	
141	- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
142	- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
143	- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
144	- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.

1	# The specification
2	
3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
4	
5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
8	
9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
10	
11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
12	
13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
14	
15	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
16	
17	## Changing the text: the revision form
18	
19	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
20	
21	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
22	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
23	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
24	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
25	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
26	
27	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
28

For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.

<!-- The record lines rung T of climb batch 31b earns, for the gather to fold. Nothing here edits FACTS.md, the gap ledger, PLAN.md, POSITIONS.md, INDEX.md or the handover. The commits are those of the branch wip/rung-tuple-parameter: f91e6b9ee7 (rows 992, 832, 819, 397) and ee53014cf2 (row 840). -->

# Rung T: the record

## Findings

1. **A compiled method's JVM parameters follow its declaration.** One parameter of a declared tuple type is the tuple's elements, one JVM parameter each, and the body makes the tuple again (`CodeGen.addParams`); one parameter whose declared type names a type parameter is one JVM parameter at every instance, the boxed tuple where the instance makes it a tuple, as the generic trait's interface declares it (`CodeGen.paramTypeAtInstance`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:901-924`); several parameters are one JVM parameter each. Conditions: the compiled path, at the commits named above. Evidence: `compiler_tests/TupleIndexMethodCompiled.test` passes (link, run, `PASS`) and failed on the base, 'java.lang.VerifyError … Type 'TupleIndexMethodCompiled$Arr2' (current frame, stack[0]) is not assignable to 'com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32''. What it means: a call through a generic trait's type at a tuple instance takes the tuple as one value, and a call on the object of the trait's body at the tuple type takes its elements; the code generator chooses by the declarations that the receiver's type holds (`callTakesTupleBoxed`, `CodeGen.java:7375-7407`).
2. **Two bridges join an instance's boxed tuple to a body's elements.** The code generator writes, in the class of a trait or object whose body at a tuple type shadows a generic trait's method over a type parameter, a method of the interface's boxed signature that unpacks the tuple, casts each element and calls the body virtually (`tupleElementsBridge`, `CodeGen.java:950-982`, written from `dumpOverloadedMethodChaining`, `:1537-1545`). The class loader writes, in an instantiated class, beside a method whose template's one parameter is a type parameter that the instance makes a tuple type, a method of the elements that packs them and calls it (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:119-165`), never in an interface (`:130`); it is made only where a tuple type, `LTuple⟦`, is substituted for a template parameter that was not one already (`:124-128`). Evidence: `TupleIndexMethodCompiled`'s generic cases `G[\T, nat w\]` and `Sel[\T\]`, which with the loader's earlier test ended in 'ClassFormatError: Duplicate method name "get" with signature "(…FZZ32;…FZZ32;)…FZZ32;"'. What it means: every `m[i,j]` of the one library's arrays of rank 2 and 3 has its body, the rehearsal's W15.
3. **The forwarders count JVM parameters.** The forwarder of an object's method to its mangled body, and of an inherited body, loads each JVM parameter of its own signature (`CodeGen.java:3154-3159`, `:867-870`), where before it loaded one per Fortress parameter, so a method of one pair parameter loaded self and one element. Evidence: `compiler_tests/TupleVarFieldCompiled.test` (row 397's program, promoted), old 'java.lang.VerifyError', new `PASS`. What it means: every compiled method of one tuple parameter, a setter of a tuple-typed field among them, has a working forwarder.

# Rung E, rung-numeral-block-end: the record lines

## Findings

1. **A compiled block that ends in a numeral after a local declaration, or in a tuple with a numeral element, at a declared type, now runs.** Conditions: the place fixes a type (a function's declared return type, a typed binding, a parameter, or the type of an `if`'s other branch). Evidence: before, the checker's join that converts a numeral where it stands had no case for a `LocalVarDecl`, a `LetFn` or a tuple (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:1304-1313`, `:1334-1385`), so the whole block was wrapped in the coercion, which the code generator compiled as a call of the generic coercion's closure at its uninstantiated arrow type (`CodeGen.java:7808-7819`, `:4147`): 'NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerBuiltin$v'. The join now reads both forms (`7fb38bbe30`); `four()` compiles to `iconst_4`, `FZZ32.make`, `areturn`. Tests: `compiler_tests/NumeralEndsBlockAfterDeclarationCompiled`, `BlockEndsInTupleOfNumeralCompiled`, `TupleBindingIfBranchesCompiled`, each failing on the base and passing after (`junit.sh final`: `OK (19 tests)`). What it means: rows 1014, 1030 and 1031 close; the workaround of binding the numeral to a typed variable first is no longer needed at a declared type.
2. **At a place that fixes no type the block after a local declaration keeps its numeral's own type.** `x = do`, `k: ZZ32 = 3`, `4`, `end` makes `x` a `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,4\]`: `println(x)` prints 4 on the base and after, and `y: ZZ32 = x` dies with 'NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerBuiltin$v' (`compiler_tests/XXXNumeralEndsUntypedBlockCompiled`). The default's walkers (`defaultNumeral`, `joinNumerals`, `tupleJoin`, `Functionals.scala:1259-1331`) have the same missing cases; they were left, since repairing them changes the type that a numeral takes at a place that runs today. What it means: a new row, NEW-E-2.
3. **Under the compiler's prelude `=/=` is refused at `RR32` and at `RR64`, and `=` at `RR32` overflows the stack.** `c =/= 0` for `c: RR32 = 0`, and `r =/= 0` for `r: RR64 = 0`: 'Could not check call to operator NE' (`compiler_tests/XXXNumeralNotEqualsFloatCompiled.test`); `c = 0`: 'java.lang.StackOverflowError' (`compiler_tests/XXXNumeralEqualsRR32Compiled`), since `Equality`'s `=` calls `===` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss:26`) and `===` at `RR32` calls `=` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:67`). At `NN32` and `NN64` `u = 0` is `true` and `u =/= 0` `false` (`compiler_tests/NumeralEqualsNumberCompiled`). What it means: the Effect of `revival-numerals` is narrowed (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5435-5453`); a new row NEW-E-1 for `=/=`; row 528 holds `=` at `RR32`, its line rewritten for today's failure.
4. **Kin unchanged.** `XXXAtomicExprNumeralArms` and `XXXAtomicExprNumeralBody` (row 1043), and `XXXLabelNumeralValueCompiled` (row 340), fail as before, with the same messages: the join has no case for an atomic expression or a `label`.
5. **The stages and the checker's time.** On the final code (`7fb38bbe30`'s): count `#total 0`, `#crash none`, equal to `climb-batch-31/gate/checker-count.txt`; distance `DISTANCE SAME   0`, no site in `errors.tsv`. Time of the count stage, one run each in one session: base 109.5 s, change 98.4 s; equal tables and equal `run.txt` after the paths are masked. A JFR profile puts 3 of 6,876 samples in the join: no second pass.

## FACTS

**A numeral at the end of a block, or in a tuple, converts where it stands on the compiled path.** At a declared type (a return type, a typed binding, a parameter, an `if`'s other branch) the compiled checker converts a numeral that ends a block after a local declaration, and each numeral element of a tuple, by the type's own coercion of the numeral itself, so the code generator folds it into a constant (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`, `numeralResult` and `joinInto`). At a place that fixes no type, a block after a local declaration keeps its numeral's own type (row NEW-E-2). Tests: `compiler_tests/NumeralEndsBlockAfterDeclarationCompiled`, `BlockEndsInTupleOfNumeralCompiled`, `TupleBindingIfBranchesCompiled`; `XXXNumeralEndsUntypedBlockCompiled`. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-numeral-block-end/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

## Ledger

Rows closed by `7fb38bbe30` (its hash on `main` after the gather), each with its test:

- Row 1014: `ledger.py close 1014 --commit <hash> --test ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NumeralEndsBlockAfterDeclarationCompiled.test`.
- Row 1030: `ledger.py close 1030 --commit <hash> --test ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/BlockEndsInTupleOfNumeralCompiled.test`.
- Row 1031: `ledger.py close 1031 --commit <hash> --test ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/TupleBindingIfBranchesCompiled.test`.

Row 528, its whole new line, for `ledger.py rewrite 528` (its claim's failure is now a stack overflow, no longer an `AbstractMethodError`; linted by `ledger.py check --rows`, no failure):

| 528 | on the compiled path the prelude's `RR32` takes its `=` from `Equality`, which calls `===`, whose declaration at `RR32` calls `=`, so `a = b` over two `RR32` values, `a = 1.5` or `c = 0` compiles clean and overflows the stack when it runs | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | library gap vs spec (prelude) | silent | `ProjectFortress/library_tests/XXXRR32EqualityRungV.test` | climb batch 6.5b rung V | siblings: 529, NEW-E-1. At 647163a9c4 the prelude's `RR32` declares only its numeral coercions (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:955-958`), `Equality`'s `=` is `(self === other)` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss:26`) and `opr ===(a:RR32, b:RR32)` is `a=b` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:67`): 'java.lang.StackOverflowError' in `XXXRR32EqualityRungV` and in `compiler_tests/XXXNumeralEqualsRR32Compiled`, a numeral zero. A program the checker accepts must not die in the JVM. Repair: the one library's `RR32` at the switch-over (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-rr32-sibling/REPORT.md` section 11); P-37 adds no prelude declaration. Workaround: bind `r: RR64 = c` and compare `r`. |

New rows, for `ledger.py add` (linted by `ledger.py check --rows`: each fails only the number rule, for its `NEW-` placeholder). Their placeholders stand also in `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5450` (`rows~NEW-E-1 and~528`) and in row 528's line above (`siblings: 529, NEW-E-1`).

NEW-E-1, section "7. Numerals, floats and comparisons", beside row 528:

| NEW-E-1 | on the compiled path, until the switch-over, the prelude's `RR32` and `RR64` declare no `=/=`, so the checker refuses `c =/= 0` for `c: RR32 = 0`, and for an `RR64` zero, 'Could not check call to operator NE', where walk answers `false` | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | library gap vs spec (prelude) | `basic/operators/opr-overview.tex`, "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators" | `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNumeralNotEqualsFloatCompiled.test` | climb batch 31b rung E | siblings: 528. At 647163a9c4 the prelude's `RR32` declares only its two numeral coercions (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:955-958`), its `RR64` no `=/=` (`:893-953`), and `Equality` only `=` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss:25-27`), where each integer type declares its own `=/=` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:784`, `:850`). Walk answers `false` at `RR32` (`ProjectFortress/tests/NotEqualNumeral.fss`). P-37 adds no prelude declaration: it ends at the switch-over, which turns the test red. Workaround: at `RR64`, `NOT (r = 0)`; at `RR32`, bind `r: RR64 = c` first, since `c = 0` meets row 528. |

NEW-E-2, section "12. The compiled path: constructs, crashes and the switch-over", beside row 1014:

| NEW-E-2 | compiled, a numeral that ends a block after a local declaration, at a binding without a declared type, keeps its numeral type, so a later conversion of the variable dies: `x = do`, `k: ZZ32 = 3`, `4`, `end`, then `y: ZZ32 = x`, 'NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerBuiltin$v' | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (checker) | `basic/expressions/blocks.tex`, "Do Expressions" | `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNumeralEndsUntypedBlockCompiled.test` | climb batch 31b rung E | siblings: 1014. The checker's default at a place that fixes no type (`defaultNumeral`, `joinNumerals` and `tupleJoin`, `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:1259-1331` at 7fb38bbe30) has no case for a `LocalVarDecl` or a `LetFn`, so `x` is a `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,4\]`: `println(x)` prints 4, and `y: ZZ32 = x` calls the coercion as a function value. The same block ending in `(1, k)`, bound and taken apart, dies with a `ClassCastException` of an `FZZ32` to a numeral type. Walk prints 4 for both. At a declared type the numeral converts where it stands (`NumeralEndsBlockAfterDeclarationCompiled`). Workaround: declare the binding's type. |

No note on row 1043 or row 340: their tests did not change.

## Handover line

Rung E is on `wip/rung-numeral-block-end` (code at `7fb38bbe30`): the compiled checker converts a numeral that ends a block after a local declaration, or stands in a tuple, where it stands at a declared type, so rows 1014, 1030 and 1031 close with their tests promoted; `ant testFast` green (compiler track 1677, 0 failures), count 0 and distance 0 with `#crash none`, the checker's time unchanged (109.5 s, 98.4 s); the compiled test of `u = 0` at `NN32` and `NN64` is written, `=/=` at `RR32` and `RR64` refused (NEW-E-1) and `=` at `RR32` overflowing the stack (row 528, rewritten) recorded, and the Effect's sentence narrowed; the same block at an untyped binding keeps its numeral type (NEW-E-2); the atomic and `label` kin (rows 1043, 340) stand.

## Revival change

Revival change: none. The change makes the compiled path do what the team's specification says and walk already does: a block's value is its last expression's (`Specification/basic/expressions/blocks.tex:54-56`), and a tuple's coercion is distributed element by element (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:829-830`). That a numeral converts where it stands, by its type's coercion of the numeral itself, is the revival's numeral design, whose departure from the team's sources is recorded with it; this change only carries that design into two more places on the compiled path, with no value that differs from what the team's compiler would have computed for the same block.

6df780a7d0 The compiled code casts self where it stands at a type below its trait

Climb batch 31, rung K (rows 991 and 695). The checker reads a comprises
clause at the level of values, so in trait Q comprises { R } self may
stand where R is expected, and in a self-typed trait self may be returned
as the implementing type. The code generator emitted no cast there, and
the JVM's verifier refused the class when it loaded. It now casts a value
that has self's type to a declared type strictly below its trait, at a
single argument, a typed binding, an assignment and a method's returned
value, also where the value is a typecase whose arms are each self.
Appendix I's sentence on a default body that returns self says that it
runs. Rows 1050 to 1053 are new: a closure's returned self, a
conditional's arm, a call on a value of the self-type parameter, and an
assignment of a subtype's value to a var field from outside its object.

This commit edits the original tree.

- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## A consolidation

A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. After a batch lands, the record-landing workflow consolidates its entries (`references/batch.md`, "The landing").

- In a consolidation, by hand or by the clarity or mining workflow, run a pilot of three or four entries first. Show their new texts to the curator as a page, each with its old text (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). Run the rest on the curator's go. The pilot shows the curator the form: the length, the register, and what belongs in the history. The other checks, the pass's step 3, the tools' cold readers and the quiz, test only the meaning. The record-landing workflow takes no pilot, since it lands with no step of yours.
- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;

11	## What changed and why
12	
13	The code generator passes a parameter of a declared tuple type as the tuple's elements, one JVM parameter each, and the body makes the tuple again (`CodeGen.addParams`). A generic trait's method over a type parameter takes one value, so at an instance that makes the parameter a tuple its interface declares one boxed tuple. Nothing joined the two, and the forwarders counted Fortress parameters, not JVM parameters. Five repairs in `CodeGen.java` and one in the class loader:
14	
15	1. The forwarders count the JVM parameters of their own signature: the object's method to its mangled body (`generateFunctionalBody`, :3154-3159) and the forwarders of inherited bodies (`generateForwardingFor`, :867-870). Before, a method of one pair parameter loaded self and one element, the VerifyError of rows 992 and 397.
16	2. `generateForwardingFor` computes a forwarded method's signature at its instance by its declared shape (`paramTypeAtInstance`, :901-924): a parameter whose declared type names a type parameter stays one JVM parameter when the instance makes it a tuple.
17	3. Where a body at the tuple type shadows a generic trait's method over a type parameter, the class gets a bridge from the interface's boxed method to the body (`dumpOverloadedMethodChaining`, :1537-1545; `joinsTupleElements`, :930-948; `tupleElementsBridge`, :950-982). The bridge unpacks as `evalArg` does and casts each element.
18	4. A dotted call passes its tuple argument boxed where every declaration that the receiver's type holds at that arity takes it so (`callTakesTupleBoxed`, :7375-7406, in `forMethodInvocation`, :7316-7322). A generic dotted method of one parameter is called with the receiver and the tuple as two values, as its closure is declared (`genericMethodTakesOneParameter`, :7354-7373; `receiverPrependedDomainType`, :7333-7351; the call, :7258-7261 and :7296-7299). Rows 992 (through the trait's type) and 832.
19	5. An operator applied to one tuple operand passes the tuple's elements, as a function call does (`forOpExpr`, :5651-5667). Row 819.
20	6. The class loader's twin is made only where a tuple type is substituted for a template parameter that was not a tuple already (`Instantiater.java:124-128`). Without it, the bridge of a generic object at a tuple type got a twin that duplicated the object's own method ('ClassFormatError: Duplicate method name "get" with signature "(…FZZ32;…FZZ32;)…FZZ32;"' on a probe of the library's shape, `G[\T, nat w\]`); with `Tuple⟦` in place of `Tuple`, the twin is no longer made for a class of a component whose name begins `Tuple`, row 840's cause.

22	## The convention as built
23	
24	A compiled method's JVM parameters follow its declaration:
25	
26	- one parameter of a declared tuple type: the tuple's elements, one JVM parameter each; the body makes the tuple again;
27	- one parameter whose declared type names a type parameter: one JVM parameter at every instance, the boxed tuple where the instance is a tuple, as the generic trait's interface declares it;
28	- several parameters: one JVM parameter each, a tuple among them boxed;
29	- a generic dotted method's closure: the receiver, then the declared parameters one each, so its one tuple parameter is boxed (`convertGenericMethodToClosureDecl`).
30	
31	Where the instantiated signature and the body's differ, two bridges join them. The code generator writes, in the class that gives a body at the tuple type, a method of the interface's boxed signature that unpacks the tuple and calls the body virtually (`tupleElementsBridge`). The class loader writes, in an instantiated class, beside a method whose template's one parameter is a type parameter that the instance makes a tuple, a method of the elements that packs them and calls it (`Instantiater.visitMethod`). A dotted call chooses the boxed form by the declarations that the receiver's type holds (`callTakesTupleBoxed`); a call through an interface finds only the boxed form, so it must. A function or operator call passes the elements, as before.

If you're working on tasks that would benefit from tracking progress, consider using TaskCreate to add new tasks and TaskUpdate to update task status (set to in_progress when starting, completed when done). entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored

So after the switch-over the code generator still stands between the library and bytecode. - F-361 **With the five number traits merged with their objects in a scratch tree, the checker count and the distance stay 0, microGPT's quick checks pass, and walk's suite differs in one `XXX` test; on `832f7d0d91`'s code the merge widens three gaps, fixed since, to the five types.** The merge makes `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` value objects (F-360): 12 files, the library's text and 78 lines of walk's Java, with no checker or code-generator file and no model line. Of the 830 tests of `ant testSystem`, 829 pass, and `XXXGenericBesidePlainReturnParam` passes where a failure is expected (row 550), for a wrong reason: walk's load check loses a refusal for a generic beside a plain declaration at an object type (row 998). The other two gaps: a type parameter bounded by a value type through a trait's generic method (row 997, passed in the scratch tree by one line of walk), and the checker's refusal of a valid generic-beside-plain pair over an object domain (row 542, by reading). A `typecase` arm that names a removed object, such as `Int`, matches every value with no message (row 959). On `main` the five traits are not merged, and rows 998, 997 and 542 are fixed. Measured once on `832f7d0d91`; nothing landed, and no test holds it; the compiled tests and `ant testFast` were not run. Detail: `compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/number-object-merge.md`, "Measurements" and "Obstacles, in the order met".

- F-344 **Under walk, a value of the five native number objects or of the four string objects is read at its trait where walk infers a static argument, and walk's type text prints each of the nine by its trait.** `Int`, `Long`, `BigNum`, `Float` and `UnsignedLong` of `FortressBuiltin` read and print as `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `RR64` and `NN64`; `FlatString`, `CatString`, `EmptyString` and `SubString` as `String`; also inside tuple types; each told by its declaring component (`interpreter/evaluator/types/LanguageTypes.java`), at `EvaluatorBase`'s three reads and in `FTraitOrObject.toString`. So `Cell(3)` is a `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, `Cell("s")` a `Cell[\String\]`, `<|1, 2, 3|>` an `ArrayList[\ZZ32\]`, and messages and `Reflect` print `ZZ32` where they printed `Int`; a float numeral, an `RR64` value (F-341), reads at `RR64`. The types keep their names: a `typecase` arm `Int` still matches `3`, and the ilk still names a string object by its own name, `FlatString`. Test: `tests/LanguageTypeInstancesWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-language-types/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-328 **Walk answers the compiled helpers `stringOps.typeName` and `equality.sEquiv` with its own operations, and its ilk names the five native number objects by their traits.** The one library binds `Object.ilkName` to `stringOps.typeName` and `SEQV` over `Any` to `equality.sEquiv` (P-58's form); walk's loader maps the two names, before it looks for a helper, to `ObjectPrims$ClassName` and `AnyPrim$SEquiv` (`interpreter/glue/NativeApp.java`, `OWN_OPERATIONS`, a table that holds `runtime`'s six names too, F-335), so it never loads the two helpers. `Object.asString` is `self.ilkName`. Walk's ilk prints `Int`, `Long`, `BigNum`, `Float` and `UnsignedLong` of `FortressBuiltin` as `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `RR64` and `NN64`, also inside static arguments, tuples and arrows; other types, strings, `Char` and `Ratio` among them, keep their names, and walk instantiates a generic at the trait (F-344). Tests: `tests/AnyNativesIntrinsicWalk`, `compiler_tests/AnyNativesIntrinsicCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-any-carrier/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-360 **In the interpreter's library each of the five number traits `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` has exactly one object, a native object of `FortressBuiltin`, and the 56 bodies of `trait RR64` that go through `asFloat(self)` run only at a type assumption, `asif RR64`.** The objects are `Int`, `Long`, `BigNum`, `UnsignedLong` and `Float`. The split was made for `IntLiteral` and for nesting (`fca589bbb0`); the flat tower and the numerals' own types removed both. At every call without `asif` the object's own declaration is more specific, so the trait's body does not run: with a `fail` put into each of the 56, walk's suite fails one test, `tests/asifTest.fss:102`, `(3.0 asif RR64) + 17`. Each such body calls the object's body on `asFloat(self)`, which is `self`, so it computes the same value. Under walk an object of a native component takes its values from the Java class of the object's name in the component's package (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildNativeEnvironment.java:42-57`), so a hand-written class as an object's class is walk's rule, and walk reads such a value at its trait (F-344). Measured once, in a scratch tree on `832f7d0d91`; the walk rule read in the code. content.content:
- F-307 **The small rest's eight native bindings name their helpers of `nativeHelpers/`, and walk's values are unchanged: `Long`'s and `BigNum`'s `asString` and `asExprString`, `NN32`'s and `NN64`'s `signed`, `Char`'s `codePoint` and the top-level `char`.** They are at `LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:389`, `:391`, `:524`, `:545`, `:547`, `:595` and `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1080`, `:4711`; the four over `NN32`, `NN64` and `Char` name the special names that the checker reads at those types (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:369-380`). `signed` above the signed half wraps, as a low-bits name does (F-331), and `char` keeps a code point outside 0 to 1114111, as the glue classes did (row 857). The top-level `printlnWithThread` and `getProperty` are natives over `FlatString` on helpers, beside overloads over `String` that flatten (F-299). Test: `tests/NativeHelperFamilySmallWalk.fss` and `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilySmallCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-natives-small/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-306 **Under walk, trait `ZZ64`'s 26 and trait `ZZ`'s 22 native bindings name helpers of `nativeHelpers/`, keep every value the glue classes gave, and their `DIV` by zero throws `DivisionByZero`.** The 48 (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:878-985`, `:1089-1195`) name 29 helpers of `simpleLongArith`, `simpleIntArith`, `simpleUnsignedLongArith` and `simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith`, those that the compiler's prelude binds for the same operations, and 11 new ones, four of `REM` and `MOD` (F-312) and seven of the divisors, `ZZ`'s `CHOOSE` and `cmp` (F-314); `ZZ64`'s four wrapping bindings name the wrapping helpers that the prelude binds under its `BOX` spellings (row 348). `longOverflowingDiv` and `div` raise the library's `DivisionByZero` under walk (F-24); `REM` and `MOD` name the new helpers, and raise `DivisionByZero` at a zero divisor too (F-312). A `ZZ` helper takes only a `BigNum` value, since walk's loader unboxes a `BigInteger` by `getBigInteger`; walk's coercions convert another integer operand first. Test: `tests/NativeHelperFamilyIntegersWalk.fss`, `tests/ZZ64DivisionByZeroWalk.fss`, `tests/ZZDivisionByZeroWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyIntegersCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-natives-integers/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-311 **`Int`'s, `RR32`'s, `NN32`'s, `Long`'s and `BigNum`'s `asFloat` answer `RR64`, as each type's own `asFloat` declares in its api (F-324), and name `nativeHelpers`' `intToDouble`, `floatToDouble`, `unsignedIntToDouble`, `longToDouble` and `toDouble`; walk's values are unchanged.** The specification: `numbers.tex:61`. At `Float`, the team's declared result, the checker refused the move ('Function body has type RR64, but declared return type is Float.'); walk carries both in a `double` and answers the same `Float` object (F-303). `longToDouble` and `toDouble` are new, `(double) a` and `a.doubleValue()`. Tests: `tests/NativeHelperFamilyAsFloatWalk`, `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyAsFloatCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-natives-asfloat/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-313 **The compiled path prints an `NN32` or `NN64` unsigned and negates an `NN64` by wrapping, and `UnsignedLong`'s `self` takes the `NN64` transfer, so `UnsignedLong`'s three bindings, `NN64`'s prefix `DOTMINUS` and `NN32`'s `CHOOSE` name helpers.** `FNN32`'s `toString` and `asString`, `FNN64`'s `toString` and `simpleUnsignedLongArith.unsignedLongToString` print unsigned; `unsignedLongWrappingNeg` answers 0 minus its operand, wrapped; the new `unsignedLongToDouble` answers an unsigned long's nearest double, ties to even, as walk's glue does; the rewrite reads an argument declared `UnsignedLong`, walk's object of `NN64`, through the `NN64` argument transfer. Under walk the five keep the glue classes' values; on the compiled path the prelude's `NN64` printing and prefix `BOXMINUS` move with the helpers. Test: `compiler_tests/UnsignedPrintingCompiled`, `UnsignedLongToStringHelperCompiled`, `NN64WrappingNegationHelperCompiled`, `NativeHelperFamilyUnsignedCompiled`; `tests/NativeHelperFamilyUnsignedWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-natives-unsigned/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why".

- F-323 **The floats' natives over `Number` and `AnyIntegral` are declared at `RR64` or convert in Fortress, and group 3's six name one-line helpers.** `random`, `Float`'s `atan2`, `printThreadInfo` and the `RR64` trait's `^` and `atan2` take an `RR64`, which coercion reaches from a `ZZ32`, an `RR32` or a numeral; another number type writes `asFloat(x)` (P-165). `Float`'s power over `AnyIntegral` converts its exponent by each type's own `asFloat` around a public bare `^` at `ZZ32` on `simpleDoubleArith.doublePowInt` (P-162). `Float`'s and `RR32`'s mixed powers, `Float`'s floor and ceiling brackets, and `FlatString`'s `=` and `flatConcat` at a `Char` name new helpers that compute as their glue did, `flatConcat` past U+FFFF keeping the low 16 bits (row 872). `printThreadInfo` at `RR64` is Fortress through `asString`, so a numeral prints as a float, `3.0`. F-299 and F-32 give the library's counts of bindings. Test: `tests/NativeHelperFloatMixedWalk`, `tests/NativeHelperRationalArgumentWalk`, `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyFloatMixedCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-natives-float-number/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 5 and 6.

35:## The checker and the one library
94:- F-90 **In the interpreter's library, several array and matrix declarations and `SUFFIX_SUM` are written so that the compiled checker accepts them: `__DefaultVector`, `__DefaultMatrix` and `TransposedMatrix` declare the array family's bound `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`, which F-151 owns; `__immutableFactory1` is declared to answer an `ImmutableArray1` (its branch for lowest index 0 is cast to that type, F-264); `__ImmutableSubArray1` has no `put`; `Matrix`'s `mul` writes its two parallel calls, once a tuple typed `((), ())`, as a parallel `do … also do … end` block, typed `()`; and `TransposedMatrix`'s `add`, `subtract` and `negate` call `Matrix`'s operators.** The unary operator `SUFFIX_SUM` on a `ZZ32` array (`FortressLibrary.fsi`) loops over `seq((0 # (|x| - 1)).reverse)`, since a strided range `a:b:c` is declared `Range[\ZZ32\]`, which is no generator, so the checker refuses `seq(a:b:c)` (row 661, open). The same change made `String`'s `left` and `right` answer `Just(c)` (P-53, built), and `QQ`'s `ceiling` and `truncate` raise `DivisionByZero` at +∞, −∞ and 0/0, P-54's present rule; P-54's later change, after the switch-over, is still to build. The distance stage shows that the checker accepts these declarations: none of its sites is in them (F-53, which lists the five). Under walk, `tests/TransposedMatrixAndFreeze.fss` checks the values of `mul`, of the factory's callers `replica` and `freeze`, of the sub-array and of the transposed arithmetic, and `tests/IntegerOrderNumerals.fss` checks `SUFFIX_SUM`'s; no test covers the bound. `tests/StringPieces.fss` and `tests/NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss` check the `String` and `QQ` parts. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-slips/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6.
176:## The harness and the gate
200:## Landed semantics
261:- F-341 **Walk's numeral is its default, carrying the numeral's four numbers, and converts from them where its place fixes a type.** An integer numeral is a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, a radix-point numeral the `RR64` nearest its value, one value per site (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java`). At a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter, a declared return type and a coercion it converts through the place type's coercion from `NaturalNumeral` or `RadixPointNumeral`, run with the four numbers bound as values of type `ZZ`, one result per site and type; a folded constant at a library number type converts from its exact value, outside the coercion; a numeral out of the type's range, one that rounds to an infinity at `RR32` or `RR64`, one at a type with no coercion from it, or one outside its coercion's `where` clause is refused there when it runs; a store keeps its default alone. Dispatch fits it at its default, unless its own coercion reaches a declaration strictly below, which then runs (F-366), else by its own type's coercions only, and reads a tie at the default; a type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default holding them all. So `q: QQ = 0.1` is 1/10 and `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed 0.5, and `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`, by `QQ`'s `=`, which the numeral reaches by its own coercion, not the library's `=` over `Any` (F-366; `tests/NumeralEqualsNumberWalk`). At load walk refuses a numeral type written as a type that a trait or an object extends, or as a static argument; one in a `comprises` clause loads (row 981). Tests: `tests/NumeralTypesWalk.fss`, `NumeralOwnTypeWalk.fss`, `NumeralNoCoercionRefusedWalk.fss`, `NumeralAtReturnWalk.fss`, `NumeralWhereRefusedWalk.fss`, `NumeralFoldedConstantLibraryWalk.fss`, `NumeralRoundsToInfinityWalk.fss`, `NumeralPointRoundsToInfinityWalk.fss`, `NumeralPointRoundsToInfinityAtParameterWalk.fss`, `NumeralFoldedRoundsToInfinityWalk.fss`, `NumeralTypeExtendedWalk.fss`, `NumeralTypeStaticArgumentWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-types/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why"; `compile-ladder/rung-static-numerals/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why"; `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-leftovers/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why".
267:- F-366 **On both paths a numeral at a call leaves the declaration that fits it at its default only for one that its own coercion reaches and whose declared parameter types lie strictly below, by subtyping.** It builds P-46's rule for a numeral at a call. P-46 does not word the order: the worker that built the rule chose subtyping, and the curator has read that choice as landed and let it stand, without wording a decision of his own. So `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true`, and `u =/= 0` is `false`, for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`; `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`; `k(5)` runs `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`; a `case` clause `0` matches a zero `NN32`; and a program's own number type with a numeral coercion compares with a numeral by its own `=`. `Equality[\T\]` declares `opr =/=(self, other:T)` as the negation of the type's `=` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:102`), which a type that extends `Equality` reaches before the `=/=` over `Any` (`:98`). The order between the declaration that the default fits and one that the coercion reaches is subtyping on the declared parameter types, not the coercion chapter's relation: `f(1.5)` beside `f(x: RR32)` and `f(x: RR64)` runs the `RR64` declaration, and `x^2` for an `RR64` keeps its integer power. A value's coercion is not ranked so. Where a call reaches two declarations only by coercion and they are not ordered, the one whose parameter the numeral's default fits as it is runs, whether they differ at the numeral alone or elsewhere too, so `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` checks against the one library at `RR64`'s juxtaposition. So a model line may compare a number of any type with a numeral, and write a float numeral beside an integer value, on both paths. The checker compares only where the declaration that fits has a numeral at a parameter that is not of the numeral's default type, so a call such as `i + 1` costs nothing more; the report says which choices walk keeps in its dispatch cache. Two departures: under walk a numeral beside a value typed `Any` is converted by the value's run-time type (row 1016), and on both paths a numeral at a bare type parameter's declaration does not go to a more specific one (row 1017). Source: `numeralAttempt` and `numeralTie` in `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:980-1021`, `:1066`, `:1117`; `bestMatchForNumerals` and `belowByNumerals` in `interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:2422-2525`. Tests: `compiler_tests/NumeralMostSpecificCompiled`, `compiler_tests/NumeralTieDefaultCompiled`, `tests/NumeralMostSpecificWalk`, `tests/NumeralEqualsNumberWalk`, `tests/NotEqualNumeral`. Every compiled top-level variable is initialized at its first read, not at load as under walk, so a binding of wildcards alone never evaluates its right side (row 1011). ## What changed and why

The base is 647163a9c4. The rung's commits on `wip/rung-numeral-block-end`: `7fb38bbe30` (the checker's edit and the tests), `20fe9f78c5` (Appendix I's sentence), `19e7e678e8` (the refusal test widened to `RR64`, and its new name in that sentence). One launch worked the rung.

**The cause as found.** A function's body is checked by `checkExpr(body, rt, ...)` (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:230`). The block passes the expected type to its last element without converting it (`impls/Misc.scala:435`), and after a local declaration that last element is a `LocalVarDecl` (or a `LetFn`) whose own body is the rest of the block. So the block's type is the numeral's own 

The bytecode of `four()` on the base (`javap -c -p Four.class`, the jar of `bin/fortress compile Four.fss` on the base's code):

    8: iconst_4

    : > "$OUT/summary.tsv"
    for f in $LIST ; do
      n=${f%.fss}
      case "$n" in
        wordcount2) ( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 15 600 bin/fortress ProjectFortress/demos/$f < /dev/null ) > "$OUT/$n.txt" 2>&1 ; rc=$? ;;

        *) timeout -k 15 600 ../../bin/fortress $f < /dev/null > "$OUT/$n.txt" 2>&1 ; rc=$? ;;
      esac
      if grep -qi fail "$OUT/$n.txt" ; then fl=fail-in-output ; else fl=clean ; fi

    done
    echo "demos: $(grep -c . "$OUT/summary.tsv") run, $(awk -F'\t' '$2=="END"' "$OUT/summary.tsv" | wc -l) reached their end"

**The checker's driver over one demo.** It runs from the tree's root, as steps 1 and 2 of `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh` with the one target:

1. Make `$S/shadow-src` with `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/shadow-patch.py ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress $S/shadow-src && python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/add-patch.py $S/shadow-src`.
2. Compile the seven shadow sources and `DistanceMulti.java`, as `run.sh:102-112` does.
3. Run the driver:

       java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow -Djava.io.tmpdir=$S/tmp -Dfortress.caches=$S/caches \
            -Dprobe.tolerant=true -Dprobe.all=true -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false \
            -cp $S/shadow-classes:$S/classes:$CP DistanceMulti -order check -setting any ProjectFortress/demos/trips.fss

`CP` is the class path that `run.sh` makes from `bin/fortress_classpath`. The driver's own line reported 53 s for the target before the repair, under `nice -n 19`, nproc 4.

\EXP{=} of \library, whose parameters are of type \TYP{Any} and which the
numeral fits at its default: at a call a numeral goes to the most specific
declaration that takes it (\secref{coercion}).
The interpreter answers \EXP{u = 0} \VAR{true}, and \EXP{u \neq 0}
\VAR{false}, for a zero \VAR{u} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} or
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, and the compiled path does so for a zero of
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} or \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}; \TYP{Equality} of \library\ declares
\EXP{\neq} as the negation of the type's own \EXP{=}, and the compiled path's
own library declares \EXP{=} and \EXP{\neq} on each integer type with an
operand of that type (\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralEqualsNumberWalk.fss},
\nolinkurl{NotEqualNumeral.fss} and \nolinkurl{NumeralMostSpecificWalk.fss};
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NumeralMostSpecificCompiled.fss} and
\nolinkurl{NumeralEqualsNumberCompiled.fss}).
At \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} the compiled path's own library declares no \EXP{\neq},
and its \EXP{=} is the one of its \TYP{Equality}, which calls that library's
\EXP{\sequiv}, whose declaration at \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} calls \EXP{=}: so for
\EXP{c\COLON\mathbb{R}32 = 0} the compiled type checker refuses
\EXP{c \neq 0}, and \EXP{c = 0} compiles and overflows the stack when it runs

\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NumeralNotEqualsFloatCompiled.fss},
and the expected failure \nolinkurl{XXXNumeralEqualsRR32Compiled.fss}, which
asserts \VAR{true}).
